patient.chief_complaint: Sudden thunderclap headache while washing dishes, 30 minutes ago, vomiting, neck stiffness
patient.history_present_illness: Mrs. Cooper is a 67-year-old woman with hypertension, type 2 diabetes, and chronic kidney disease stage 3 who presents with a sudden onset catastrophic headache that began while doing the dishes at home. She describes it as an instantaneous explosion, rated 10/10, the worst headache of her life. She vomited twice and her husband called 911. She has marked neck stiffness and photophobia on arrival. She has had no prior severe headaches. She manages multiple comorbidities including CKD stage 3 with eGFR 42, which is clinically relevant for two reasons: contrast-induced nephropathy risk for CTA, and electrolyte disturbances (especially hyponatremia) which may complicate her SAH course given her baseline CKD. Her candesartan (ARB) will have an additive hypotensive effect with nimodipine, requiring it to be held. Metformin must be held after IV contrast administration due to risk of contrast-induced nephropathy and subsequent lactic acidosis. Her furosemide will also contribute to electrolyte loss and requires monitoring. She is insulin-dependent and hyperglycemia management will be important in the ICU. Her blood pressure on arrival is severely elevated despite her antihypertensive medications.

output.query: CKD stage 3 contrast induced nephropathy prevention SAH CTA

results.finding: eGFR 42 (CKD stage 3) - moderate risk for contrast-induced nephropathy
IV hydration with isotonic saline before and after contrast most effective prevention
Minimize contrast volume - discuss with interventional radiology
Hold metformin 48h post-contrast in CKD to prevent metformin-associated lactic acidosis
N-acetylcysteine: uncertain benefit; not routinely recommended by KDIGO 2023

output.summary: Patients with CKD stage 3 (eGFR 30–59 mL/min) face moderate risk for contrast-associated acute kidney injury following iodinated contrast administration. IV isotonic saline hydration before and after contrast is the most consistently supported preventive measure. Minimizing contrast volume reduces cumulative nephrotoxic exposure. N-acetylcysteine is not routinely recommended per KDIGO 2023 due to uncertain benefit. Metformin-associated lactic acidosis is a rare but serious complication in patients with renal impairment who receive contrast; guidelines recommend holding metformin around the time of contrast administration and until renal function is reassessed. Clinical correlation recommended.

results.finding: Hyperglycemia in SAH increases vasospasm risk and worsens outcomes
Target glucose 140-180 mg/dL in ICU SAH patients
Avoid hypoglycemia <80 mg/dL - may worsen cerebral ischemia
Insulin infusion protocol preferred for glucose >180 mg/dL
Metformin held during contrast and critical illness - adjust insulin accordingly

output.summary: Hyperglycemia in the setting of aneurysmal subarachnoid hemorrhage is independently associated with increased vasospasm risk and worse neurological outcomes. Published guidelines and observational data support a glucose target of 140–180 mg/dL in the neurocritical care setting. Both hypoglycemia (<80 mg/dL) and marked hyperglycemia worsen cerebral ischemia. Insulin infusion protocols are commonly used for glucose levels persistently above threshold. Clinical correlation recommended.
